# Exercise art — every draw command

**Complete: all 190 exercises are drawn** (finished 2026-09-01), generated by
hand in ChatGPT, one shared style. This file stays as the recipe for drawing
new exercises as they get added — the style primer below, one line per
exercise naming what separates it from its neighbours, then `art.mjs`.

Names put the weight form in trailing parentheses — `Bench Press (Dumbbell)`,
not `Dumbbell Bench Press`. That is how the database reads, and the filenames are
derived from it, so the two cannot drift.

**You do not need to name or save files in any particular way.** Hand over the
sheets in any order; each one is identified by what it depicts.

---

## Paste this once, at the start of the conversation

The style below is not aspirational — it describes what ChatGPT already produces.
Pasting it back is what keeps the new 80 matching the existing 110.

> You are going to draw a series of exercise illustrations for a workout app.
> Every image must share one identical house style, because they appear together
> in a list and any drift is obvious.
>
> **Style, fixed for every image in this conversation:**
> - A single 3D-rendered anatomical figure — a muscular male mannequin in matte
>   light grey, no face, no hair, no clothing beyond plain trunks. Soft studio
>   lighting, visible muscle definition, no skin colour and no texture detail.
> - The muscle being worked is a solid red-orange (#E0362A) directly on the
>   figure's body, in the anatomically correct place. It is the only saturated
>   colour in the image.
> - Equipment — barbell, dumbbell, machine, cable, bench — rendered in near-black
>   matte metal so it reads as present but never competes with the figure.
> - Background: solid black, edge to edge. No gradient, no floor, no wall, no
>   shadow cast on anything, no gym.
> - Whole body in frame, captured mid-repetition at the position that makes the
>   movement recognisable. Face the camera unless the exercise only reads from
>   the side.
> - Absolutely no text, letters, numbers, labels, arrows, logos or watermarks.
>
> **Every request I send will be a sheet of four exercises**, and you must return
> them as one square image divided into an even 2 × 2 grid — one exercise per
> quadrant, filling its quadrant. I will always list them in the order top-left,
> top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right, and you must place them in exactly that
> order.
>
> **Three rules about the sheet that matter more than anything else:**
> 1. The image must be **square** — equal width and height. Never widescreen.
> 2. Exactly **four** figures, never more. Do not draw a second view, a variation,
>    or an extra angle of any exercise.
> 3. One figure per quadrant, and no figure may cross a quadrant boundary. No
>    dividing lines, borders, gutters, captions or numbering.
>
> **The test that matters:** each quadrant will be displayed at 44 × 44 pixels.
> Shapes must be bold and well separated. Anything thin, fussy or fine-detailed
> disappears at that size, so simplify aggressively.
>
> Reply "ready" and then I will send the first sheet.

If a sheet comes back wrong, reply "again, but ..." in the same conversation
rather than starting over; it keeps the style anchored. To redo a single
exercise, send its one line with "Draw this one alone, as a single square image."

---

## The one rule that matters

**Say what separates a variant from its neighbours.** Across 110 drawings this is
the only instruction that reliably changed the output. Left to itself the model
draws a group of variants as one picture repeated — three cable flys came back
identical, and an arm sheet once returned two preacher curls and three
near-identical cable curls instead of the four exercises asked for.

What is left is one sheet and two single redos, and the rule still applies —
sheet 16 has two machines that ChatGPT loves to draw as the same machine, and
both redos below failed exactly this way the first time.

**Check the four you get back are the four you asked for** before moving on.

---

## What happens to the sheets

Hand them over and they get sliced, downscaled to 512, named and committed. The
slicer is `tools/art.mjs` — no dependencies, since this repo has no build step.

```
node tools/art.mjs sheet <image.png> <top-left> <top-right> <bottom-left> <bottom-right>
node tools/art.mjs sheet <image.png> --cols 3 <left> <middle> <right>
node tools/art.mjs single <image.png> <slug>
node tools/art.mjs region <image.png> <slug> <x> <y> <w> <h>
```

The slicer measures and trims the divider ChatGPT sometimes draws between
quadrants, and ignores any bright band too wide to be one — that check exists
because a 3 x 1 strip once triggered an 80px trim and cost a swimmer both feet.

## Second positions — the other end of the movement

Each drawing shows one end of the rep. A second drawing at the other end, shown
alternating with the first in the exercise sheet, is how the movement gets
across — the way Hevy and ExRx do it. A video model was tried first (see
`exercise-videos.md`); it put the bar through the figure's neck.

**The 46 exercises in the current routines**, listed below with what the
existing drawing shows and what the second one must. The rest of the library
can follow the same way.

The second drawing is filed beside the first as `<slug>-2.png`, and the app
picks it up the moment the file exists, exactly like the first. The slicer has a
command for it — full size only, no thumbnail, because lists never animate:

```
node tools/art.mjs second <image.png> <slug>
```

### Paste this once, at the start of the conversation

The existing drawing goes in as an attachment every time, so the style is
carried by the image rather than by the description. What the primer has to fix
is everything *except* the pose, because the two drawings are shown one over the
other and any drift between them — camera, framing, equipment — shows as a jump.

> I am going to send you drawings from a set, one at a time, and ask for each one
> redrawn with the figure at the other end of the movement — the position I
> describe with it.
>
> Everything else must be identical to the drawing I attach: the same camera
> angle and distance, the same framing, the same figure, the same equipment in
> the same place, the same lighting, the same red-orange highlight on the same
> muscle, the same solid black background. Only the body's position changes, and
> only as much as the movement requires. The two images will be shown alternating
> in the same spot, so anything that moves besides the body will visibly jump.
>
> Return one square image. No text, labels, arrows or watermarks.
>
> Reply "ready" and I will send the first one.

### Then send each one like this

> **Same image, other end of the movement:** arms locked out straight, the bar held high above the chest.

with the drawing attached. Check the framing matches before slicing — hold the
two side by side. A figure that has shifted or a bench that has grown is a redo,
and "again, but keep the camera exactly where it is" is usually enough.
